key_points: Upper airway obstruction frequently presents to the interventional bronchoscopist with causes including malignant tracheal disease and postintubation stenosis.
Physiological changes are due to turbulent airflow at stenosis, leading to increased resistance, higher work of breathing, hypoventilation, and exercise limitation.
Characteristic changes are seen on pulmonary function tests, especially flow-volume loops.
Fixed obstruction shows plateauing of inspiratory and expiratory limbs, differentiating it from variable intrathoracic or extrathoracic obstruction.
Spirometry and quantitative indices (e.g., FEV1/PEFR ≥ 10, FEV1/FEV0.5 ≥ 1.5) are useful but lack sensitivity; bronchoscopy and imaging are essential.

diagnostic_approaches: Flow-volume loop analysis: fixed obstruction shows plateauing of both limbs.
Quantitative indices: PEFR:PIFR ratio, MEF50:MIP50 ratio, FEF50%/FIF50% ≥1, FEV1/PEFR ≥10 ml/l/min, FEV1/FEV0.5 ≥1.5.
Impulse oscillometry: resistance (R) constant across frequencies in fixed obstruction.
Heliox trial: improves turbulent flow obstruction but not COPD-related laminar obstruction.
Imaging: CT, MRI, virtual bronchoscopy for lesion characterization.
treatment_algorithms: Initial stabilization with heliox in acute obstruction.
Surgical resection for select tumors or stenoses.
Definitive management guided by etiology (malignant vs benign vs postintubation).
clinical_guidelines: Flow-volume loops are useful but lack diagnostic sensitivity; bronchoscopy is required for confirmation.
In COPD patients, absence of plateau does not rule out fixed obstruction.
FEV1/FEV0.5 ratio <0.6 suggests central obstruction over COPD.
Stridor and dyspnea unresponsive to bronchodilators should prompt evaluation for fixed obstruction.
drug_information: Heliox (60–80% helium, 20–40% oxygen) reduces turbulence and dyspnea in acute obstruction.

clinical_pearls: Flow-volume loop plateauing of both limbs is the hallmark of fixed obstruction.
Heliox reduces turbulent flow and work of breathing, useful as a bridge in acute obstruction.
FEV1/FEV0.5 <0.6 helps differentiate central obstruction from COPD.
Impulse oscillometry shows resistance independent of frequency in fixed obstruction.
Failure to respond to bronchodilators in wheezing/stridor should raise suspicion.

clinical_applications: Flow-volume loops and spirometry are inexpensive but lack sensitivity; use for screening.
Bronchoscopy and CT imaging remain the diagnostic gold standards.
practice_recommendations: Suspect fixed obstruction in patients with unexplained stridor, wheeze, or dyspnea unresponsive to bronchodilators.
Always confirm with bronchoscopy and imaging.
future_directions: Further validation of spirometric indices in real-world patient populations.
Expanded use of impulse oscillometry and non-invasive imaging.
controversies: Sensitivity of physiologic tests remains low; criteria derived from simulations may not reflect real-world accuracy.

points: Fixed airway obstruction persists throughout the respiratory cycle and produces characteristic plateauing on flow-volume loops.
Symptoms include exertional dyspnea, stridor, and wheeze unresponsive to bronchodilators.
Pulmonary function tests are suggestive but lack sensitivity; bronchoscopy and imaging are required.
